caption_hook: Texas has dinosaur tracks, a fossil reef, a salt dome and the granite of Enchanted Rock.

layers.name: OGALLALA FORMATION
layers.hook: The sand sheet under the plains
layers.what: Rivers from the Rockies spread sand and gravel into a hard cap that holds up the Llano Estacado. The Ogallala Aquifer below waters much of the Panhandle.
layers.bonus: Farmers pump the aquifer far faster than rain can refill it.

layers.name: GLEN ROSE LIMESTONE
layers.what: Dinosaurs walked a muddy tidal flat that later turned into limestone. Their tracks are still visible in the Paluxy River at Dinosaur Valley State Park.
layers.bonus: Both a long-necked sauropod and a three-toed predator left tracks side by side.

layers.name: LOUANN SALT
layers.hook: The salt that pushed up oil
layers.what: The young Gulf of Mexico basin dried up and left a thick salt bed. Salt flows slowly upward like toothpaste, doming the rock above it and trapping oil.
layers.bonus: Spindletop, a salt dome near Beaumont, gushed in 1901 and launched the Texas oil boom.

layers.name: CAPITAN LIMESTONE
layers.hook: A fossil reef you can hike
layers.what: A giant reef grew along the edge of a Permian sea, and it now stands in the Guadalupe Mountains. It is one of the best-preserved fossil reefs on Earth.
layers.bonus: Guadalupe Peak, at 8,751 feet, is the tallest point in Texas.

layers.name: BARNETT SHALE
layers.what: A black, gas-rich shale from an ancient sea lies deep under North Texas. In the late 1990s, drillers cracked it open and kicked off the modern shale boom.
layers.bonus: Fort Worth sits right on top of it, with wells even in city parks.

layers.name: TOWN MOUNTAIN GRANITE
layers.what: Molten rock cooled underground as ancient continents collided. Erosion has since exposed Enchanted Rock, a huge bare granite dome in the Hill Country.
layers.bonus: At night the rock groans as it cools, which gave it its name.
